title: Socialisation
examples: Can you give an example of a norm I might learn at school?
What is the difference between a value and a norm?
How does the media act as an agent of socialisation?

explain.say: Today we are learning about socialisation. Say this word with me: socialisation.
The family is often the first agent of socialisation. Say this: primary agent.
Schools are another important agent of socialisation. Say this: secondary agent.
Norms are the expected behaviour rules in a group. Say this: unwritten rules.
Values are the ideas about what is good or important. Say this: shared beliefs.

draw.text: Values: What is important to us

explain.say: In real life, when you see litter on the ground, you know to pick it up. This shows a learned norm.

faq.q: What is the main difference between a norm and a value?
faq.a: A value is a broad belief about what is good or right. A norm is a specific rule about how you should act because of that value.
asks: Can you give an example of a value guiding a norm?

faq.q: Does socialisation only happen in the family?
faq.a: No, socialisation happens everywhere we interact with people. Schools, friends, and the media all teach us things.
asks: Are there other agents besides the family?
Does the media teach us anything?

faq.q: What is the role of the primary agent?
faq.a: The primary agent, usually the family, teaches us our very first language and basic social behaviours.
asks: Who is the most important agent?

faq.q: Are norms the same as laws?
faq.a: No, laws are written rules enforced by the state. Norms are often unwritten expectations within a community.
asks: Is a norm always a law?
What is the difference between expected and required?

faq.q: Can a person learn different norms in different cultures?
faq.a: Yes, culture dictates many of our norms. What is polite in one place might be unusual in another.

facts: The family is considered the primary agent of socialisation.
Secondary agents include schools, peers, and the media.
Values are abstract ideas about what is desirable.
Norms are the specific rules guiding behaviour in a society.

quiz.say: If a society values honesty, which of these is a possible norm?

options.show: Being truthful only when it helps you.
options.say: Being truthful only when it helps you.

options.show: Always telling the truth, even when difficult.
options.say: Always telling the truth, even when difficult.

options.show: Only telling the truth to adults.
options.say: Only telling the truth to adults.

quiz.why: This is a specific behaviour rule (norm) that supports the general belief (value) of honesty.

wrong.0: This is a reaction to being caught, not the general rule of honesty.
wrong.1: This describes self-interest, not the core value of honesty.
wrong.3: This is too limited; honesty applies in all situations.

quiz.say: Which agent is responsible for teaching formal subjects like mathematics?
quiz.why: Schools provide structured learning in specific subjects like maths and science.

wrong.1: While families teach things, they do not teach formal subjects like algebra.
wrong.2: Peers influence behaviour, but they do not teach structured academic content.
wrong.3: The media can show examples, but it does not teach structured lessons.

quiz.say: A student always waits for their turn to speak in class. This behaviour is most likely governed by:
quiz.why: Waiting your turn is a specific, expected rule of behaviour in that setting.

wrong.1: A value is a belief, like 'respect', not the action of waiting.
wrong.2: This describes the source, not the type of rule itself.
wrong.3: This describes the source, not the type of rule itself.
